I'd be happy to talk more about that if there is interest, or provide summaries of papers and clinical trials for a lay person to understand. However the purpose of this post will be talking about COVID and the testing methods used.

The test is based on a technology called polymerase chain reaction (PCR). It is a technique used to amplify DNA that is very well established and has been used for quite a long time. There is a derivative called qPCR in which you quantify DNA for a given sequence. You can use specific primers to amplify only sections of DNA you want, and quantify the amount of each sequence. Primers are about 20 base pairs in length and you use forward and reverse primers for each strand of DNA. You design primers based on a sequence that is unique to a particular gene so you won't get amplification or other genes. This is used to differentiate different genes within one organism, NOT compare between related ones. What I mean is, you use qPCR to test levels of your genes of interest in say, human samples compared all other human genes. If I have, say 5 genes I think might be expressed at a higher rate in some disease, I test those genes and I can tell them apart from any other genes in the human genome.

This is not true for the SAME gene in different organisms. If you take a human gene, many other animals will have a very similar gene. Primates have most of the same genes and they are 99% the same in sequence as well. It would be very hard to use qPCR to tell apart human from chimpanzee. This is a stupid example because you'd never have this, but say I mixed chimpanzee and human samples together in one and wanted to tell the levels of the same gene but be able to tell apart levels from each species, qPCR wouldn't be the choice. I would need to use the more expensive RNA sequencing which analyzes each nucleotide identity. PCR costs maybe $1-5 per sample, RNA seq costs $200-1000. My point in saying all this is you can't properly tell apart very close species from each other with qPCR.

Now I don't know the sequence of COVID compared to related coronaviruses, but I suspect they are likely 99% the same. Unless you choose primers in regions that are unique to COVID, AND show you don't get cross amplification with other species, you cannot say that you have identified COVID-19. All you have done is shown presence of some similar virus. So unless I'm mistaken and they have REALLY good qPCR primers that are highly specific, there's no way these tests are good for telling apart covid from any seasonal coronavirus. This is all workin in the assumption COVID-19 is even real which to be honest I'm not 100% certain of.

No promises but I may be able to. I would then check the databases and align the sequence to similar coronaviruses and compare them, see how similar and if this is a truly novel coronavirus.
